content: Acute otitis media (AOM) typically develops following a viral upper respiratory tract infection, which causes Eustachian tube dysfunction. This dysfunction impairs the clearance of secretions and disrupts pressure regulation in the middle ear. Current guidelines recommend observation rather than immediate antibiotic therapy for children aged 6 to 24 months with unilateral AOM without otorrhea, as well as for children older than 2 years with either unilateral or bilateral AOM without otorrhea. Observation is appropriate if close follow-up can be ensured, and antibiotics can be initiated if symptoms persist or worsen within 48 to 72 hours. The most common bacterial pathogens associated with AOM include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae. High-dose amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day) is the first-line antibiotic treatment for AOM. If the patient does not respond to initial therapy within 48 to 72 hours, high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate or intramuscular ceftriaxone should be considered. The optimal duration of antibiotic therapy for AOM remains uncertain. A 10-day course is recommended for children younger than 2 years or those with severe symptoms. For children aged 2 to 5 years without severe symptoms, a 7-day course is advised. For children aged 6 years and older without severe symptoms, a 5-day course is generally sufficient. Pain management is an essential component of AOM treatment. Mild to moderate ear pain (otalgia) is typically managed with acetaminophen or ibuprofen. For severe otalgia, narcotic analgesics containing codeine may be used, but with caution due to the risks of respiratory depression, altered mental status, gastrointestinal upset, and constipation. Immediate antibiotic therapy is particularly beneficial in cases of bilateral AOM, AOM with severe symptoms (e.g., moderate to severe otalgia lasting at least 48 hours or a fever of 39°C or higher), AOM with otorrhea, or infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. When initiating antibiotic therapy, high-dose amoxicillin is recommended if the patient has not received amoxicillin in the past 30 days, does not have concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, and is not allergic to penicillin. If any of these criteria are not met, additional β-lactamase coverage (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate) should be considered. In cases of recurrent AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin, or if the patient has received amoxicillin in the past 30 days, or has concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, alternative antibiotics with broader coverage should be used. Tympanocentesis may also be considered in refractory or complicated cases.
